knight_criteria.rationale: Interstellar distance ('sixty-odd light-years') and geological prospecting for metals, oil, and gas are referenced, but scientific facts are only lightly invoked as backdrop rather than materially explored.

Successive Earth technologies--interstellar spaceships, telegraph, printing presses, gas appliances, radio, television, concrete--materially drive the plot by displacing Zurian industries and enabling the takeover.
The story concerns contemporaneous interstellar contact on an alien world; there is no future, remote past, or temporal displacement materially represented.

The whole narrative extrapolates the consequences of an identifiable premise--Earth's overpopulation and its economic method of conquest via trade, credit, and technology--culminating in the total takeover of Zur.
No character materially applies observation, hypothesis, testing, or evidential revision to drive understanding; economic maneuvering is not scientific method.
The story is set on the alien planet Zur and centrally features visitors from Earth arriving via interstellar spaceship; the other-world setting and off-world visitors are foundational.

The complete economic and cultural takeover of an entire planet constitutes large-scale human-caused dislocation, but it is deliberately non-violent and framed as gentle, so its status as a catastrophe is interpretively uncertain.
